Distinguished Chairperson, distinguished delegates, the issue of space debris mitigation is a key factor for the long-term safety of spaceflight. The instruments currently adopted on that matter consolidate international efforts on space debris mitigation. However, they are inadequate in the face of the fast pace of evolution of space activities that we see today. Firstly, the instruments are not legally binding. Secondly, they barely touch upon international law aspects and are solely focused on technical measures. Finally, they focus solely on prevention and ignore matters related to removing existing debris. Some states are actively promoting the concept of responsible conduct in space, in accordance with which a space vehicle has only to be defunct or non-functioning for it to be considered for removal. For the Russian Federation, this simplified approach is unacceptable. Only the state of registration has the right to deem a space vehicle defunct. This raises the need to craft and adopt legally significant definitions of the terms space debris and space debris object. We also call for the drafting of international standards on managing the lifecycle of space vehicles, including on minimizing their impact on orbital space. That implies strict compliance with space vehicle service life, measures to prevent space debris from arising in near-Earth space due to the active existence of a space vehicle ceasing, and also measures to mitigate further space debris, including on the moon and other celestial bodies. By way of conclusion, in the current context of continuous growth in the number of space operators and orbital constellations in near-Earth space, We must secure strict compliance with international space law and the relevant COPOS recommendations when space projects are implemented. Thank you.

Mr. President, Chairperson, distinguished delegates, the space debris mitigation guidelines elaborated by this committee were a very timely initiative in terms of addressing the growing challenges posed by space debris. The Compendium of Space Debris Mitigation Standards on the USO website shows that states do undertake measures to mitigate space debris in line with the Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines. Canada recommends that all states consult the compendium regularly and provide up-to-date information. The compendium also contains information on measures implemented by other states that states can draw inspiration from. The Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines provide international— internationally accepted standards that can be applied by all states in a manner adapted to their space activities and their regulatory framework. The flexible nature of international standards means that they can be updated and refined as new technology emerges and the space debris situation evolves. The efforts currently underway to promote application of the 21 guidelines on the long-term sustainability of space activities is also aligned with an approach that seeks to evolve and adapt to the situation in outer space and offers great potential for addressing the challenges we face. However, space debris mitigation measures alone will not be sufficient to address the challenges. posed by debris congestion in outer space, in order to ensure the long-term sustainability of space activities, active removal could become necessary. Such activities raise major legal implications. For example, precise identification of the state of registration, the launch state or states, the state of the owner and operator of any space object earmarked for removal is essential in order to ensure that consent is obtained from all of them. There are also important issues of liability in the context of debris removal attempts. The Liability Convention provides for agreements assigning liability between joint launch states of a single space object. In the context of debris removal, agreements assigning liability between the launch state and the state of the space object conducting the removal and the launch state of the space object for removal would also be useful. Of course, this is subject to the Liability Convention's reservation concerning the right of a state offering damages, or rather suffering damages, to seek compensation from one or other of the relevant launch states. Finally, the potential for harmful interference in the peaceful activities of other states not directly involved in the debris removal It cannot be ignored. An attempt to remove a space debris object carries inherent risks of damage to the targeted space object, but also to other nearby space objects, and can lead to additional debris. For that reason, it can be relevant or even useful to use the mechanism, the consultation mechanism of Article 9 of the Outer Space Treaty, so as to involve a broader group of stakeholders before moving forward.

It's a priority for France in the framework of work within COPRO. France has long been involved in initiatives seeking to mitigate space debris. CNES is also actively contributing to the updating of ISO 24113 on space debris mitigation requirements. Chairperson Frans is of the view that international regulatory efforts have allowed considerable progress and need to be pursued, deepened, and flanked by national efforts. In line with Article 6 of the Outer Space Treaty, states bear international responsibility for national activities in outer space. The conduct of such activities requires the issuance of a license based on compliance with binding technical requirements, notably when it comes to space debris mitigation. In 2024, France updated its national technical regulations so as to strengthen the requirements on combating space debris alongside already integrated measures such as non-generation of debris during the nominal maneuvers of a space object. Regulatory efforts need to be flanked with research and innovation efforts to provide technical solutions that will allow operators to meet their obligations. Thank you, Chair. For New Zealand, effective debris mitigation and remediation is supported by 3 main tools: a national authorization system, transparency measures, and non-binding international instruments that help put existing international space law obligations into practice. Under New Zealand's national authorization system, operators seeking permission to launch launch payloads from New Zealand must show how they plan to reduce the creation of debris across the entire life of their mission. This is done by submitting a debris mitigation plan that follows internationally recognized guidelines. New Zealand has also developed domestic regulatory policy to support active debris removal and in-orbit servicing missions. This policy provides a clear pathway for assessing novel and complex missions, including those involving proximity operations or interaction with other space objects, while managing safety and security risks. This approach promotes transparency and safety and seeks to enable activity that supports sustainability. New Zealand recognizes that debris mitigation should not be limited to Earth orbit. This is reflected in domestic policy settings for lunar missions, which include requirements to plan for post-mission disposal. New Zealand has also developed a non-binding arrangement with the United Kingdom to support cooperation on active debris removal and in-orbit servicing activities. This arrangement shows how states can address legal uncertainty associated with debris remediation missions, including by promoting cooperation, transparency, and shared approaches to legal risk while operating within the framework of existing international space law. Thank you, Chair.
I thank New Zealand for their statement, and now I give the floor to South Africa.

Chairperson, South Africa regards the proliferation of space debris as a clear example of how sustainability in outer space has become a legal issue, not merely a technical one. Existing mitigation guidelines remain important, and we welcome the extent to which they have informed national regulation. At the same time, the present environment of congestion, congestion and collision risks suggest that mitigation alone is no longer sufficient. The legal discussion must now engage more directly with remediation, including active debris removal, and with the question this raises in relation to jurisdiction, consent, liability, and standard of responsible conduct. South Africa notes in this regard that other developing countries have also recognized remediation as a necessary part of the discussion, while stressing that it must be approached through a consultative and multilateral process. South Africa's view is that the next stage of the legal discussion should be more precise. It should be acknowledged that Article 8 of the Outer Space Treaty and the continued jurisdiction and control of the State of Registry place real legal constraints on remediation measures. At the same time, prolonged inaction in relation to defunct objects imposes growing costs on all users of the space environment. The legal task is therefore to give practical effect to due regard and international cooperation in circumstances where the risk is shared but legal control remains attached to individual states. In that regard, South Africa considers that notification, consultation, Consent and coordination will remain central to any future multilateral guidance on remediation measures. Chairperson, South Africa also considers that the legal treatment of debris cannot ignore questions of equity. The current debris environment was not created equally, and future legal responses should reflect that reality. In our view, view, greater attention should be given to differentiated responsibilities and capabilities, particularly in relation to the cost of compliance, access to data and technology, and support for developing countries in implementing debt-related obligations. South Africa knows that the G77 and China have similarly called for common but differentiated responsibilities in the context of remediation, and for those actors, for those actors most responsible for creating debris to be most actively involved in removal efforts and in sharing relevant expertise with developing countries. In conclusion, South Africa will therefore support continued work towards practical multilateral guidance on remediation measures. Including notification, consent, coordination, and liability-related questions. Pending the development of more specific legal mechanisms, non-legally binding guidance may continue to play a useful supporting role, but such guidance should remain firmly within an inclusive multilateral process and should not obscure The need for a more coherent legal response to the long-term sustainability challenges now facing the space environment. Thank you.

Such mechanism would, first, continue discussions on the legal and policy aspects of space traffic coordination and management in a manner that complements the ongoing work of the SDSC, in particular the LTS Working Group and its Expert Group on Space Situational Awareness, without prejudice to its independence. Germany reiterates its commitment to supporting the establishment of a dedicated working mechanism under this agenda item with the legal subcommittee. To facilitate consensus at the committee meeting in July, we invite the subcommittee to schedule informal consultations in the intercessional period. Thank you for your kind attention.
I thank Germany for that statement, and now I give the floor to Ukraine.

Distinguished Chair, distinguished delegates, the management of space traffic constitutes a key aspect of ensuring the long-term sustainability of space activity. However, current development trends such as the significant increase in the number of satellite operating in relatively limited orbital regions, the polycentricity of the governmental space situation awareness centers that predominantly cooperate through bilateral arrangements, and the growing commercialization of the system through the data exchange among operators, and the use of the artificial intelligence for the large-scale data processing to support collision avoidance decisions, indicate the need for the resilient and interoperable ecosystem of space traffic management network governed by the minimum transparency standard, shared risk protocols, and inclusive access. In the— in this context, it may be considered that the future legal norms can be designed to establish an interoperable governance model supported by the data sharing mechanism in which mandatory national licensing requirements play a significant role. Such requirements should ensure that each operator possesses the technological capability to rapidly and interoperably disseminate information regarding its position and maneuvers. Furthermore, increasing importance should be attached to the legal regulation of the data reliability as well as to the development of the common criteria for such reliability at the international level, with subsequent implementation in the national legal framework. Taking this into consideration, Ukrainian delegation expressed its support for the continued development of the legal mechanism aimed at implementing of UN Long-Term Sustainability Guidelines and AEDC Technical Guidelines, as well as the initiative on the legal and policy aspect of space traffic within the legal subcommittee of COPUS.

Thank you, Mr.

Chair.
I thank Ukraine for their statement. I give the floor to the United Kingdom.

Thank you, Chair. The United Kingdom welcomes this opportunity to exchange views on the legal aspects of space traffic management. We recognize the increasing urgency of this discussion as space becomes more congested and complex, and as reliance on space services continue to grow across our economies and societies. The UK understands space traffic management to be a set of technical, operational, regulatory measures that support the safe and sustainable conduct of space activities throughout the full lifecycle of space objects. Effective space traffic management is underpinning by robust space situational awareness, which enables operators and authorities to understand risk and hazards in the space domain, manage complexity, and support safe and sustainable space operations. Space domain awareness is therefore a priority for the United Kingdom and a critical enabling capability for the coordination of space traffic. We are developing technologies and partnerships to enhance our abilities to monitor, track, characterize objects in, in orbit with the aim of reducing collision risk, preventing harmful interference, and protecting critical space infrastructure. These efforts support our wider policy objectives on space safety, sustainability, and resilience. We strongly support continued discussions within the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee committee, including the work of the expert group on space situational awareness coordination. The United Kingdom has submitted information on national practices in this area and welcomes the contributions made by others. We encourage further voluntary submissions to help build a clear picture of existing approaches, practical challenges, and areas of convergence. Looking ahead, the UK sees great value in a pragmatic and inclusive approach to space traffic focused on improving coordination, transparency, and information sharing between operators and relevant authorities. This should build on the existing practices, support reasonable behavior in space, and remain adaptable to technology— technological change and the evolving space environment. The United Kingdom looks forward to continued constructive engagement with partners, and this work progresses within the subcommittee. Thank you.
I thank the United Kingdom for their statement, and now I give the floor to Austria.

Thank you, Mr.

Chair.

As orbital environments become more and more congested, space traffic incidents and near misses are increasingly common. 14,000 active satellites and 1.2 million debris objects larger than 1 centimeter are crowding critical orbital planes. OSCE remains convinced that COPOS and its subcommittees are the key fora to address the challenges of space traffic in a comprehensive manner. The challenge is both technical and legal. Therefore, both the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee, including on Space Situational Awareness, as well as this legal subcommittee have important roles to play. Austria regrets that it was not possible to agree on a more structured format within the legal subcommittee to advance this work, including in the form of a study group. Together with a group of countries in which all of the United Nations regional groups were represented, it supported the establishment of such a study group last year. The topic certainly remains important and urgent, and we just made meaningful progress this year. We would like to thank Germany for its efforts in compiling and summarizing the contributions made by delegations. In its submission, Austria made reference to its national regulatory framework, which reflects key obligations of responsible space actors. These include safety and continuous supervision of space activities, mitigation of space debris, as well as planned termination and safe end-of-life scenarios. Austria also supports the increased efforts of the European Union to develop an EU approach to STM and is deeply embedded in space surveillance and tracking at EU level. National and regional efforts in space traffic management are important, in particular in the absence of a global system. However, they will only be able to ensure safety and collision avoidance to a certain extent. Austria will therefore continue to support all efforts and initiatives aimed at strengthening international cooperation in this regard. It emphasizes the need for a successful global system for traffic management, just as it has been achieved at sea or in aviation. Improving space safety and security through global traffic management is not just an option, it should be a common priority for all of us. Thank you, Mr.

Chair.
I thank Austria for their statement, and I give the floor to the Russian Federation.

Distinguished Chairperson, space traffic management is a very important aspect of ensuring the safety and sustainability of space activities. In view of the increase in the number of space objects, including satellites and fragments. We need to develop frameworks that would allow for space traffic management. We need to develop rules and standards, mechanisms and principles that would allow us to avoid collisions and ensure the safety of existing objects and future ones. The availability of precise information on space objects and events is critically important to space traffic management. And to preventing incidents in orbit. Collecting and exchanging such data improves the safety of space operations and cooperation in this area. Increased density of space objects requires better cooperation in this area. We need to set up a system of monitoring and information exchange between states so as to identify risks and adopt measures to prevent them. In this connection, the Russian Federation welcomes the use of an open platform for data exchange under the auspices of the UN so as to ensure better transparency and safety in space. We must avoid monopolization of sources of information on events in space. A key area for space traffic management is to have information on objects and planned maneuvers. The Russian delegation under this item has submitted proposals. These are reflected in the draft guidelines on the long-term sustainability of space activities and also in our CRP, CRP 13, entitled A UN Information System as an Expanded System for Realizing Competencies in the Sphere of Furnishing Information on space objects and events for common use. The proposed platform is to be used to integrate states' efforts and those of international organizations, operators, relevant national and international non-governmental bodies in the area of gathering, systemizing, and providing for common use and analysis of information on space objects and events. As part of discussion of this topic, we need to bear in mind that in many cases such information can be quite sensitive for states. Additionally, we must also discuss the criteria for timeliness, reliability, and accuracy of such information, the procedure for provision of information and access to it by interested users, and also responsibility by for suppliers for the accuracy of data and for the timely provision of information. We would also like to note that we don't know of any state in which road, water, or air transport would be based— or their management would be based on non-legally binding recommendations. If we join up our efforts, we can ensure that we meet our objectives in space traffic management. We urge all countries to participate in the development of legal instruments that will ensure the safety and sustainability of space activities and allow us to address the challenges related to space traffic management.

Thank you.
